title: Symphony of Shadows
tagline: He lives under Beethoven's shadow and finds his own towering voice.

scenes.text: Vienna, 1876. Johannes Brahms is 43 years old and has not yet written a symphony. The ghost of Beethoven looms over him — 'the footsteps of a giant,' he calls it. Tonight, after twenty-one years of drafts and doubts, he premieres his First.

scenes.speaker: Johannes Brahms
scenes.text: You cannot hear what I hear before I write it down. The music exists perfectly in my mind — and then degrades as I put it on paper. A composer's tragedy is that the ideal is always just beyond the real.

challenge.instruction: Twenty-three years before this premiere, the young Brahms joined Schumann in writing a sonata on a friend's motto. Turn the wheel until Joachim's motto reads.
challenge.fact: Robert Schumann heard the 20-year-old Brahms play in 1853 and immediately published an article declaring him 'the one called to give ideal expression to the times.' It was an extraordinary endorsement that launched Brahms' career — and also set impossible expectations that would haunt him for decades.

scenes.text: Brahms was Clara Schumann's closest friend and champion of her husband Robert's music after Robert's breakdown and death. His relationship with Clara — intense, complex, never consummated — shaped his most personal compositions.

challenge.instruction: Before any symphony, Brahms made his name with a requiem written after his mother's death. Arrange the movements of A German Requiem in order.
challenge.fact: Brahms labored over his First Symphony for 21 years, from 1854 to 1876. He was paralyzed by the shadow of Beethoven — convinced that any symphony he wrote would be compared unfavorably to Beethoven's nine. When it finally premiered, the conductor Hans von Bülow called it 'Beethoven's Tenth' — the highest compliment and a backhanded burden.

scenes.speaker: Johannes Brahms
scenes.text: They say I am a conservative — a reactionary against the New German School. Wagner and Liszt may have their future. But counterpoint, structure, the sonata form — these are not antique fetters. They are the bones of music.

challenge.instruction: Brahms hears tempo in the structure of the music, not in a ticking machine. Still, pick out every pendulum that truly beats with the reference — only its length sets the time.
challenge.fact: Brahms was his own harshest critic. By his own account he wrote some twenty string quartets before he let one be published — the pair of Op. 51, in 1873 — and he burned many drafts and early works he judged unworthy.

challenge.instruction: The song Brahms wrote for a friend's newborn became the world's lullaby. Play it through as the strings press the tempo.
challenge.fact: Brahms's Wiegenlied was first sung in public in Vienna in December 1869, with Clara Schumann at the piano. Few melodies have been sung over more cradles since.

challenge.instruction: Edison's agent has carried a phonograph to Vienna to catch the master at the piano. Gear the motor down so the wax cylinder turns true while Brahms plays his Hungarian Dance.
challenge.fact: On 2 December 1889 Brahms played part of his first Hungarian Dance into Edison's phonograph in Vienna. The worn cylinder, copied many times since, is the only recording of Brahms himself at the keyboard.

scenes.speaker: Johannes Brahms
scenes.text: This time the whole board is judged at once. Deploy George Bernard Shaw, Coco Chanel and me, turn us public, then declare the Roadshow: the highest public Culture on the board when the round ends takes the prize.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 6 · Global Competition. Deploy your Great People, Go Public on each, then start the Roadshow and End Turn to win the round with the highest public Culture on the board.
challenge.fact: A Global Competition counts every public Great Person on the whole board; followers and face-down cards add nothing. It lasts one round, and the strongest player draws a reward: event cards, followers or a new Great Person.
